title: Exploration Maps vs ArcGIS for Mining Maps
metaDescription: ArcGIS vs Exploration Maps for mining maps: enterprise GIS power and licensing versus a focused tool for claim maps, drill figures and investor decks.
directAnswer: Exploration Maps is purpose-built for investor-ready mining maps and can produce a polished export in 15–30 minutes with no GIS training required. ArcGIS is a full GIS platform best suited for complex spatial analysis, but requires expensive licensing, significant training, and hours of configuration to produce presentation-quality map outputs.

sections.body: ArcGIS is a professional GIS platform designed for spatial analysis, data management, and complex cartography. It can do almost anything — but that power comes with steep licensing costs ($1,500–$10,000+ per year), a significant learning curve, and the need for a dedicated GIS professional to operate it effectively. Exploration Maps is a single-purpose tool: create investor-ready exploration maps quickly, without GIS expertise.

In ArcGIS, producing a presentation-quality map requires setting up a project, importing data, managing coordinate systems, configuring the layout view with title blocks and legends, and often several rounds of style adjustments. A first map typically takes 2–4 hours for someone experienced with the software. In Exploration Maps, importing data, applying a theme, and exporting a polished PNG uses a guided workflow in the browser, with no GIS installation required.

ArcGIS Pro (the standard desktop version) costs approximately $1,500 USD per year for a single named-user license. ArcGIS Online subscriptions start at $500/year. For a junior mining company producing 5–10 maps per year, this cost is difficult to justify — particularly when a GIS consultant at $75–$150/hour must also be engaged to operate the software. Exploration Maps is significantly more accessible for small teams.

sections.h2: When ArcGIS is the Right Choice
sections.body: ArcGIS is the right choice when you need complex spatial analysis: processing geophysical grids, running mineral potential modelling, managing large claim tenure datasets, or producing regulatory GIS deliverables that require specific projection standards and metadata. For these tasks, Exploration Maps is not the right tool. If your goal is producing a clean map for an investor deck or news release, ArcGIS is substantial overkill.

sections.h2: When Exploration Maps is the Right Choice
sections.body: Exploration Maps is the right choice for: investor presentations, NI 43-101 figures, exploration news release maps, property overview maps, and any situation where speed and presentation quality matter more than raw GIS capability. It is particularly well-suited to geologists and IR professionals who need to produce maps regularly but do not have GIS training.

faqs.q: Can Exploration Maps replace ArcGIS entirely?
faqs.a: For a junior exploration company that only needs investor presentation maps, news release figures, and NI 43-101 map figures, yes — Exploration Maps can handle all of these. If you need complex spatial analysis, geophysical grid processing, or regulatory GIS deliverables, you still need ArcGIS or QGIS for those tasks.

faqs.q: Does Exploration Maps support the same file formats as ArcGIS?
faqs.a: Exploration Maps imports zipped shapefiles, KML/KMZ, GeoJSON and CSV. You can import a shapefile ZIP directly, or export a layer from ArcGIS as GeoJSON. Check the coordinate system and field mapping when importing.

faqs.q: Is Exploration Maps suitable for NI 43-101 technical reports?
faqs.a: Yes. Exploration Maps can produce all required map elements for NI 43-101 reports: north arrow, scale bar, legend, title block with project name and date, and company logo. Exports are available as high-resolution PNG and PDF suitable for inclusion in technical report documents.

title: Exploration Maps vs QGIS for Exploration Mapping
metaDescription: When QGIS is the right tool for exploration work and when a focused map builder wins: spatial analysis versus presentation-ready claim and drill maps.
directAnswer: QGIS is a full open-source GIS and it is the better tool for spatial analysis, coordinate system management, raster and geophysical processing, and advanced cartography. Exploration Maps is narrower on purpose: it produces presentation-ready exploration figures — claim maps, drill collar plans, investor and news-release figures — without a desktop install or a layout composer. Most exploration teams end up using both, with QGIS for preparation and analysis and Exploration Maps for the figure that goes out.

sections.h2: What QGIS is genuinely better at
sections.body: QGIS handles coordinate system transformation and CRS management properly, does real spatial analysis, processes rasters and geophysical grids, and its print layout composer will produce any cartographic output you can specify. It is free and open source, actively developed, and it is the correct answer for most serious GIS work in an exploration company. If your problem is analytical, use QGIS.

sections.h2: Exploration Maps: Fast Output, No Configuration
sections.body: Exploration Maps is deliberately narrow. Design themes fix the title block, legend, panel colours and fonts, so producing a figure is a matter of adding data and framing it rather than composing a layout. That is a real constraint as well as a convenience — if you need a bespoke cartographic layout, a layout composer is the right tool and QGIS has one.

Most experienced exploration teams use a hybrid workflow: QGIS for data preparation, coordinate system management, and any spatial analysis (clipping, buffering, processing geophysical grids), then export the results as GeoJSON for import into Exploration Maps for final presentation-quality output. This leverages the strengths of both tools.

sections.h2: Cost, and the honest version of the trade-off
sections.body: QGIS is free, which matters to a bootstrapped junior. Exploration Maps has a free tier and a $29/month Pro tier. The trade-off is not price, and it is not quality — a skilled GIS user will produce a better map in QGIS than in anything else, given time.
sections.html: The trade-off is who is doing the work and how often. A team with a GIS specialist should keep using QGIS. A team where the geologist is also the cartographer, producing the same kinds of figures repeatedly under deadline, generally finds a narrower tool gets the figure out. Both things can be true.

faqs.q: Can I use QGIS to prepare data and Exploration Maps for the final map?
faqs.a: Yes — this is actually the recommended workflow for teams that need both analytical capability and fast presentation output. Export your processed layers from QGIS as GeoJSON (right-click layer → Export → Save Features As → GeoJSON, CRS: EPSG:4326), then import into Exploration Maps.

faqs.q: Does QGIS produce better-quality maps than Exploration Maps?
faqs.a: QGIS Print Layout can produce high-quality maps. Exploration Maps focuses on browser-based templates for investor maps and news-release figures. Compare both using your own project data, required formats and revision workflow before choosing.

cardSummary: QGIS for analysis and projection management, Exploration Maps for presentation figures. Most teams use both.

directAnswer: If you need clean, investor-ready maps quickly and without a GIS specialist, Exploration Maps is the fastest path. If you need spatial analysis, coordinate transformations, or heavy data processing, QGIS (free) or ArcGIS remain the better tools. Many teams use both: do the analysis in a GIS, then build the presentation map in Exploration Maps. Exploration Maps is a fast map-making and visualization tool, not a replacement for a full GIS.

sections.body: Junior exploration teams mostly need a specific set of outputs: investor presentation figures (16:9 PNG), NI 43-101 report maps (PDF), news-release figures, and property overview maps for decks and websites. That's a different job from the spatial analysis majors and government surveys do — and the right tool depends on which job you're doing.

sections.body: Exploration Maps is purpose-built for junior mining presentation maps. It ships investor-ready themes pre-configured with north arrow, scale bar, legend, and title block, searches public claim data, and imports shapefiles, KML, GeoJSON, and drillhole CSVs — browser-based, no GIS training. It is deliberately not a full GIS: for analysis you'll still want QGIS or ArcGIS.

sections.h2: QGIS: best free option with full GIS power
sections.body: QGIS is excellent for teams with a geologist or GIS professional. It's free, full-featured, and produces high-quality cartography and real spatial analysis — but it takes meaningful time to configure a map to presentation standard, which is exactly the gap Exploration Maps fills.

sections.h2: ArcGIS: industry standard for technical GIS
sections.body: ArcGIS is the gold standard for professional GIS in mining; most majors and geological surveys run on it. It's the better choice when you need deep analysis and enterprise data management. For a junior whose main need is presentation maps, the cost and learning curve are often hard to justify without a dedicated GIS pro on staff.

MapInfo (now Precisely MapInfo Pro) is a capable enterprise GIS used at some majors and surveys in Canada and Australia. Like ArcGIS, it's strong for technical work but carries cost and complexity barriers, with a smaller community.

Some teams polish a GIS-exported map in Illustrator for a bespoke look. Illustrator produces beautiful output but can't handle geographic data natively — it's a finishing layer, not a mapping tool, and impractical for quick, repeatable investor maps.

faqs.q: What map software do most junior mining companies use?
faqs.a: Usually a combination: QGIS or ArcGIS for data management and analysis, plus a faster tool like Exploration Maps (or Illustrator finishing) for presentation-quality outputs. The trend is toward browser-based tools that non-GIS staff can use independently for decks and news releases.

faqs.q: Does Exploration Maps replace QGIS or ArcGIS?
faqs.a: No — and it isn't trying to. Exploration Maps is a fast map-making and visualization tool for clean investor-ready and news-release maps. faqs.q: Do I need GIS software if I use Exploration Maps?

If you need to process raw survey data, transform coordinate systems, or run spatial analysis, use QGIS or ArcGIS for those steps, then export GeoJSON and import it into Exploration Maps to build the final map.

faqs.a: Search a claimholder to pull public claim data, or import your shapefile/KML/GeoJSON/CSV, assign the Claims or Drillholes role, add a branded title block, and export. See the mining claims map guide for the full workflow.

title: Exploration Maps vs MapInfo for Mining Maps
metaDescription: Comparing Exploration Maps and MapInfo Pro for mining exploration maps: which tool is faster and more practical for junior mining companies.
directAnswer: MapInfo Pro is an established enterprise GIS platform used at major mining companies and geological surveys, particularly in Canada and Australia. For junior exploration companies that need investor-ready maps quickly without a dedicated GIS professional, Exploration Maps is significantly faster, lower cost, and requires no installation or training.

sections.h2: What MapInfo Is Used For in Mining
sections.body: MapInfo Pro (now Precisely MapInfo Pro) has a long history in the Canadian and Australian mining industries — it was the dominant GIS platform at major mining companies and geological surveys before ArcGIS gained its current market position. Many exploration databases (including Geoscience BC, Ontario Geological Survey, and Geoscience Australia) distribute data in MapInfo TAB format. As a result, some junior companies inherit MapInfo-based workflows when acquiring projects from majors or accessing government datasets.

MapInfo Pro is a full-featured desktop GIS application. Producing a presentation-quality map — with a clean layout, styled title block, legend, north arrow, and scale bar — requires working in the Layout Designer module and typically takes 1–3 hours for an experienced user. For someone new to the software, expect a multi-day learning curve before producing acceptable output. Exploration Maps produces the same output in 15–30 minutes on a first use, with no training required.

MapInfo Pro is priced at approximately $1,500–$3,000 USD per year for a standard named-user subscription. This positions it in the same cost tier as ArcGIS Pro. For a junior exploration company producing maps occasionally, this is a difficult cost to justify. Exploration Maps is significantly more accessible for small teams without in-house GIS staff.

sections.h2: When MapInfo Is the Right Choice
sections.body: MapInfo Pro is the right choice if your team already has licensed users and established workflows, if you regularly receive data in TAB format from government datasets or joint venture partners, or if you need its spatial analysis and data management capabilities for managing large claim tenure databases or geoscience datasets. For these workflows, MapInfo remains a capable and well-supported platform.

sections.h2: When Exploration Maps Is the Right Choice
sections.body: Exploration Maps is the right choice for investor presentations, NI 43-101 map figures, news release maps, and property overview maps — situations where speed, presentation quality, and accessibility matter more than full GIS capability. It is particularly well-suited to junior companies without a GIS professional on staff who need polished maps on a regular basis without the overhead of maintaining an enterprise GIS licence.

rows: No (imports shapefile ZIP, KML/KMZ, GeoJSON and CSV)

faqs.q: Can I import MapInfo TAB files into Exploration Maps?
faqs.a: Not directly — Exploration Maps imports shapefile ZIP, KML/KMZ, GeoJSON and CSV. To use MapInfo TAB data in Exploration Maps, open the TAB file in QGIS (which reads TAB format natively), then export the layer as GeoJSON with CRS set to EPSG:4326. This takes about two minutes and preserves all attribute data from the TAB file.

faqs.q: Is MapInfo still widely used in the mining industry?
faqs.a: MapInfo retains a meaningful user base at major mining companies and geological surveys, particularly in Canada and Australia where it has a long established history. It is less common at junior exploration companies, where ArcGIS and QGIS have largely displaced it for new deployments. Its native TAB format remains relevant because many government geoscience data portals distribute data in TAB or MIF/MID format.

faqs.q: Can Exploration Maps replace MapInfo for investor-facing maps?
faqs.a: Exploration Maps provides browser-based layouts for investor presentations, news-release maps and property overviews. Whether it replaces your MapInfo workflow depends on the data formats, analysis and deliverables you need. Keep a GIS workflow for spatial analysis, TAB data management and GIS data submissions.

faqs.q: Does the industry expect MapInfo-format deliverables for any submissions?
faqs.a: Some government bodies and regulatory agencies in Canada and Australia request or accept MapInfo TAB or MIF/MID format for GIS data submissions. These are data deliverables (the underlying geospatial data), not map figures. Exploration Maps produces map figures (PNG, PDF) — if you need to deliver raw GIS data in TAB format, you will still need MapInfo or QGIS with the appropriate export plugin for that specific requirement.

title: Exploration Maps 3D vs Desktop 3D Software (Leapfrog Viewer, Geoscience ANALYST)
fullTitle: Exploration Maps 3D vs Leapfrog Viewer and Geoscience ANALYST | Exploration Maps
metaDescription: How a browser 3D drill figure maker compares with desktop 3D viewers such as Leapfrog Viewer and Geoscience ANALYST, and where each fits in the workflow.
cardSummary: A browser figure maker for presentation graphics, compared fairly with the desktop 3D viewers geologists already use.
directAnswer: They do different jobs. Leapfrog Viewer and Geoscience ANALYST are free desktop 3D viewers from geological software vendors, built for exploring models and data interactively alongside modelling work. Exploration Maps 3D is a browser tool (in beta) that turns collar, survey and assay CSVs into a branded, annotated 3D figure and section for news releases and investor decks. It does no geological modelling or resource estimation. Many teams will use a desktop package for the geology and a figure maker for the image that goes public.

sections.body: If your question is "what does the orebody look like and how do these holes relate to the model?", you want 3D geological software and its viewer. If your question is "what figure goes in tomorrow's news release?", you want something that produces a finished, branded, annotated image quickly and the same way every time. These overlap less than it seems, and this page sets out where each is the better tool.

Leapfrog Viewer is a free viewer from Seequent for opening and exploring scenes and models built in Leapfrog, its implicit geological modelling software. It lets people without a Leapfrog licence, such as managers, partners or reviewers, rotate and inspect the model a geologist has built. Its strength is fidelity to that model: what the viewer shows is what the modeller built.

Geoscience ANALYST is a free 3D visualisation application from Mira Geoscience for viewing and integrating geological, geophysical and drilling data, built around Mira's open GEOH5 data format. A paid Pro edition adds further tools. Its strength is bringing many data types into one interactive 3D scene.

Exploration Maps 3D runs in a web browser with nothing to install. You drop in collars, assays and optionally surveys, topography and OBJ model shapes as CSV or ZIP, and it produces a figure: terrain (with a satellite drape once the coordinate system is set), a glass or solid block with wall labels, grade-coloured traces, intercept callouts, a plan inset, a section A–A′, and export sizes for slides, news releases, social posts and A4 print, plus a layers ZIP for designers. It also has presentation-focused helpers: "Assays pending" labels, a metal-equivalent calculator that prints its formula in the footnote, a display cut-off, data checks, and an optional grade shell interpolated from assays that is labelled as an exploratory envelope.

sections.html: Geological modelling, estimation and geophysical processing remain jobs for specialist software. If a figure needs a modelled solid, export it as an OBJ mesh from the software that built it, if that software supports OBJ export, and load it as a model shape; it is drawn as supplied. For what the assay-based shell does and does not mean, see grade shells from drill assays.

sections.body: Turning a viewer screenshot into a release figure usually means a designer adding a title block, legend, scale, callouts, logo and disclosure notes by hand, then doing it again next month with slightly different numbers. A figure maker builds those elements from the data: callouts come from the assays, the legend from the colour limits, the footnote from the assumptions, and the export is the right size. The next release reuses the same project with new assays.
sections.html: The full workflow is in how to make a 3D drill hole figure.

sections.body: A team with a modeller and a current geological model already has the 3D picture; what it often lacks is a quick, repeatable way to turn that picture into a public figure with the right callouts and notes. A team without modelling software, typically early in a drill program, may only need to show holes, grades and terrain clearly, and can do that from its CSV exports alone. Reviewers can rotate and zoom an Exploration Maps 3D figure through a shared link or embed. Use a desktop viewer when the review needs the native geological model and its specialist tools. And a figure that will be published should always be checked against the source the geology came from, whichever tool drew it.

faqs.q: Is Exploration Maps 3D a replacement for Leapfrog?
faqs.a: No. Leapfrog is geological modelling software and Exploration Maps 3D does no modelling. Exploration Maps 3D makes presentation figures from drill data, and can show a modelled solid you export as OBJ.

faqs.q: Can I open Geoscience ANALYST or Leapfrog files in Exploration Maps 3D?
faqs.a: Not directly. It reads CSV tables (collars, surveys, assays, topography) and OBJ meshes, loose or in a ZIP. Export those from your software or drill database.

faqs.q: Which is better for a news release figure?
faqs.a: For a finished, branded, annotated image with callouts and disclosure notes, a figure maker is faster. For checking the geology the figure represents, use your modelling software and its viewer, and have the QP compare the two.
